text: Joshna Chinappa, born on 15 September 1986 in Chennai, Tamil Nadu, is an Indian squash player who became the youngest Indian national champion at 14, winning both junior and senior national titles. She is a two-time World Champion and four-time Asian Champion. Recognizing her contributions, she was awarded the Arjuna Award in 2013 and the Padma Shri in 2024. Her father, Anjan Chinappa, runs a coffee plantation in Coorg and was also her first coach and a member of the Tamil Nadu squash team. Her great granduncle K.M. Cariappa, the first commander-in-chief of the Indian Army in independent India, and her grandfather, father, and grandfather were all squash players. Joshna began playing squash at age seven and joined the Madras Cricket Club at eight, after deciding against badminton and tennis. She was the first beneficiary of the Mittal Champions Trust established by Mahesh Bhupati with funding from Lakshmi Mittal. In 2000, she won her first junior and senior national championships, becoming the youngest to hold both titles. In 2003, she won the British Junior Open U17 title at 16 and reached the U19 final the following year, losing to Omneya Abdel Kawy of Egypt. In 2005, she won the U17 title again by defeating Tenille Swartz of South Africa. In July 2005, she reached the finals of the World Junior Squash Championships in Belgium, losing to Raneem El Weleily of Egypt, having previously reached the last eight in 2003. In 2007, she switched coaches from Mohammad Medhaat to Malcolm Willstrop. In 2008, she won her first WISPA tour title at the NSC Super Satellite No 3 in Malaysia, defeating Low Wee Wern, and won a second tour title the following week by beating Wern again, reaching a career-best PSA World rank of 39. In 2010, she won the German Ladies Open, defeating Gaby Schmohl 11–6, 11–7, 11–6, marking her fourth tour title and first in Europe. In 2011, she won the Windy City Open by beating Dipika Pallikal 3–2 in the final. In August 2012, she faced an injury layoff during the Hamptons Open and returned in May after a seven-month break, winning the WISPA title at the 2012 Chennai Open by defeating Sarah Jane Perry 9–11, 11–4, 11–8, 12–10. In February, she won the Winter Club Women's Open; in April, she won the Richmond Open, defeating Australia's former world champion Rachael Grinham 11–9, 11–5, 11–8, her first win against her in six meetings. In March, she reached her new career-high PSA world ranking of 19. In August 2014, she and Dipika entered the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow as fifth-seeds in women's doubles, advancing through the group stage and reaching the quarterfinals, where they defeated Joelle King and Amanda Land-Murphy in straight games. They beat the second-seeded Australian pair of Rachael Grinham and Kasey Brown in the semifinals to reach the final, defeating the English pair of Jenny Duncalf and Laura Massaro in an upset win in less than 28 minutes with scores of 11–6, 11–8. This marked India's first-ever squash medal at the Commonwealth Games and made them the first Indian women to win a gold medal in squash. In May 2015, she reached the semifinals at the HKFC International but lost to Annie Au. In August, she won the Victorian Open in Australia for her tenth tour title, defeating Line Hansen 11–5, 11–4, 11–9. In September, she won the NSCI Open by beating Egypt's Habiba Mohamed 11–8, 11–9, 11–6, though she was injured during the second game after Mohamed struck her on the face with the racket. In October, she defeated Salma Hany of Egypt 11–9, 8–11, 5–11, 11–8, 11–9 to reach the semifinals of the 2015 Carol Weymuller Open, losing to Joelle King. In the first round of the Qatar Classic, she defeated Raneem El Welily, the World No. 1 at the time. In December 2015, she achieved her career-high world rank of 13, becoming the highest-ranked Indian woman player, overtaking Dipika. In February 2016, she lost in the quarterfinals of the Cleveland Classic to Camille Serme. At the 2016 South Asian Games in Guwahati as the top-seed, she won gold by defeating Maria Toorpaki Wazir 10–12, 11–7, 11–9, 11–7. In May 2016, she reached the semifinals of the HKFC International, defeating Annie Au 3–2 after losing the title the previous year, but lost in the final to Joelle King. In July, she rose to a career-high ranking of 10, becoming the second Indian to enter the world's top 10 after Dipika. In August, at the 2016 SRAM Invitational in Malaysia, she reached the finals after beating Joelle King in the semifinal but lost to Nicol David in the final. In October, she reached the finals of the 2016 Otters International in Mumbai after defeating Tesni Evans 3–1, 11–6, 15–13, 9–11, 11–8, losing to Annie Au in the final 9–11, 11–13, 7–11. In November, she participated in the 2016 World Team Squash Championships in Paris with Dipika, Akanksha Salunkhe, and Sunayna Kuruvilla, but the Indian team did not qualify for the knockout stage. In March 2017, she lost in the second round of the British Open to Raneem El Welily. In April, she participated in the 2017 Asian Individual Squash Championships in Chennai, reaching the final and defeating Palikkal 13–15, 12–10, 11–13, 11–4, 11–4, becoming the first Indian to win the Asian Squash Championship, which she described as her biggest achievement. In August, she and Dipika reached the quarterfinals of the World Doubles Squash Championship as second-seeds, defeating Samantha Cornett and Nikole Todd 10–11, 11–6, 11–8, and settled for a bronze medal after losing to Jenny Duncalf and Alison Waters. In September, she won her 15th national championship title at the 74th National Squash Championships in Greater Noida, one title short of the record. Later that month, she reached the final of the 2017 HKFC International as the third-seed but lost to Nour El Tayebl. In April 2018, she reached the quarterfinals of the women's singles event at the Commonwealth Games after defeating Tamika Saxby of Australia, but lost to Joelle King 11–5, 11–6, 11–9. Alongside Dipika Pallikal, she won the doubles silver medal at the 2018 Commonwealth Games. In April, she won her second-round match at the El Gouna International against eight-time world champion Nicol David in straight games, a notable upset. She lost in the quarterfinals. In August, she reached the semifinals of the 2018 Asian Games, defeating Nicol David 12–10, 11–9, 6–11, 10–12, 11–9, and lost to Sivasangari Subramaniam in the final, securing a silver medal. In October, she reached the quarterfinals of the Carol Weymuller Open. In March, she lost in the quarterfinals of the Black Ball Open to Joelle King. In April, she lost in the semifinals of the Macau Open. In May 2019, she won the Asian Individual Squash Championships by defeating Annie Au in the final. In June, she won her 17th national squash championship title, breaking the record previously held by Bhuvneshwari Kumari, who had won the title 16 times. In October, at the World Squash Championship, she lost to Nour El Sherbini of Egypt in the pre-quarterfinal. In February, she won her 18th national title at the 77th Senior National Championship. On 2 February 2014, she won the Winnipeg Winter Open, her maiden WSA world title, defeating Egypt's Heba El Torky 11–13, 11–8, 11–5, 3–11, 12–10. Joshna and Dipika are regarded as India's top-performing women squash players, both having reached the world's top 10. Joshna states that the rivalry between them is exaggerated by the media; they are competitive but get along well, often sharing rooms during events and competing together in events like the Commonwealth Games. Together, they won the Women’s Doubles Gold Medal at the 2022 Squash World Doubles Championships in Glasgow, Scotland.
